title: Contrastive Spectral Rectification: Test-Time Defense towards Zero-shot Adversarial Robustness of CLIP
claim: Our method retains near-clean accuracy and strongly outperforms prior defenses across diverse benchmark groups, especially under stronger attacks where baselines collapse.
layout: 2 side-by-side radar charts, left-to-right, shared legend below, 'nearly zero' callout
description: Two octagonal radar charts sit side by side. The left is titled PGD (L∞=1/255) and the right AutoAttack/APGD (L∞=4/255). Each has eight spokes: four benign categories (General, FG, Scene, Domain) with green labels and four adversarial categories (starred, red-pink labels). Four colored polygons overlay each chart: CLIP (green circles), FARE (blue squares), TTC (purple triangles), and CSR (red stars, filled pink). The red CSR polygon is the outermost shape and annotated with bold red numbers at its vertices, such as 78.7 and 39.9. On the adversarial spokes, CLIP and TTC collapse toward the center; the right chart carries a purple 'nearly zero' callout. A shared legend runs along the bottom. The eye goes first to the large red polygon.
caption: Zero-shot adversarial robustness comparison. We evaluate our \textbf{CSR} against \textbf{CLIP}, \textbf{FARE} (adversarial fine-tuning), and \textbf{TTC} (test-time defense) on 16 datasets grouped into General, Fine-Grained (FG), Scene, and Domain. The radar charts show Top-1 accuracy on \tightbox{bg-green}{benign} and \tightbox{bg-red}{adversarial} samples under standard PGD ($\epsilon=1/255$) and the stronger AutoAttack (APGD) ($\epsilon=4/255$).
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot generalization, yet remain highly vulnerable to adversarial examples (AEs). While test-time defenses are promising, existing methods fail to provide sufficient robustness against strong attacks and are often hampered by high inference latency and task-specific applicability. To address these limitations, we start by investigating the intrinsic properties of AEs, which reveals that AEs exhibit severe feature inconsistency under progressive frequency attenuation. We further attribute this to the model's inherent spectral bias. Leveraging this insight, we propose an efficient test-time defense named Contrastive Spectral Rectification (CSR). CSR optimizes a rectification perturbation to realign the input with the natural manifold under a spectral-guided contrastive objective, which is applied input-adaptively. Extensive experiments across 16 classification benchmarks demonstrate that CSR outperforms the SOTA by an average of 18.1% against strong APGD with modest inference overhead. Furthermore, CSR exhibits broad applicability across diverse visual tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/Summu77/CSR.
